newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten dodges spotlight in HK on British polling day.
newsitem.headline: Patten dodges spotlight in HK on British polling day.

text.p: The man who masterminded the Conservative Party's last election victory in 1992 was behind his desk, dodging the limelight, a world away in the colonies on Thursday, as Prime Minister John Major battled for survival.

Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten was spending Britain's election day in Government House and offering no chance for the Hong Kong press horde to corner him with questions on the future of his party and his own future as its possible new leader.
Patten, the former Conservative chairman who pulled off the 1992 election triumph for Major, had no special plans on polling day, his spokesman told Reuters. Friday would be much the same.
The poll battle is widely tipped to end in a crushing win for opposition Labour, ending the 18-year reign of Patten's party.
"He has a series of meetings, it's a normal day," the spokesman said.
It was a marked contrast from Patten's habitual community walkabouts and off-the-cuff comments to a trailing press pack, and, political analysts said, probably a deliberate retreat.

The 28th and last British governor of Hong Kong, which returns to Chinese rule on July 1, Patten said on Wednesday that Britain's policy on Hong Kong would remain the same regardless of who won the general election.
"Policy on Hong Kong has had cross-party support at Westminister," he told reporters.

But Patten, appointed governor after ironically losing his own seat in parliament in 1992, has doggedly evaded questions about his own future after he sails out of Hong Kong on the royal yacht Britannia in two months' time.

Speculation persists that he might return to parliamentary politics, as a potential leader of a defeated Conservative Party. But Patten has indicated he may take a break when his stint as governor ends, and finish writing a book.

"Dropping in and out of politics isn't like dropping in and out of the RAC motoring club," Patten told Reuters in a recent interview. "My brain and blood tells me I should spend some months recharging my batteries," he said.
He said he sees himself pondering his future for a while and spending some time "tending my garden in France" where he has a country home.
The prospect of a Labour Party victory is viewed with little concern in Hong Kong, a bastion of free trade and low taxes that has traditionally been wary of socialist policies.

A change of government could help to ease tensions between London and Beijing raised by disputes over how Hong Kong should be run after the transfer of sovereignty, the territory's main English-language daily South China Morning Post said this week.

"With so little time left before the handover, the outcome of the election will not mean much to Hong Kong, although it is possible the climate over the territory between Beijing and London could improve under a Labour government," it said.
